title: Book 5 — Terpsichore, Chapter 117
paragraphs: Daurises directed his march to the cities on the Hellespont and took Dardanus and Abydos and Percote and Lampsacus and Paesus—taking one of these on each day. But as he was marching from Paesus against the city of Parium, the report came that the Carians had made common cause with the Ionians and were in revolt from the Persians. He therefore turned back from the Hellespont and marched his army upon Caria. As it happened, a report of this was brought to the Carians before Daurises arrived; and on being informed, the Carians gathered at the place called the “White Pillars,” and at the river Marsyas, which flows from the region of Idrias and empties into the Maeander. When the Carians had gathered there, among many counsels offered, the best, in my opinion, was that of Pixodarus son of Mausolus, a man of Cindye, who was married to the daughter of Syennesis king of the Cilicians. His opinion was that the Carians should cross the Maeander and engage the Persians with the river at their backs, so that the Carians, being unable to flee backwards and compelled to remain where they were, might prove themselves even braver in the fight than they naturally would. This opinion did not prevail; they resolved instead that the Persians rather than themselves should have the Maeander at their backs—clearly so that if the Persians were put to flight and worsted, they might never return home but fall into the river.
